claims.text: A defect-inclusive predictive model will yield more accurate conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr than defect-free analytical models over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen are within the proposed model's sample domain.
Oxygen impurities and microstructural disorder produce defect-induced electron-scattering mechanisms in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen impurities and microstructural disorder produce defect-induced phonon-scattering mechanisms in HfNbTaTiZr.
Transport in HfNbTaTiZr at 0–200 K is dominated by low-energy excitations and phonon scattering.
Thermally activated defect motion becomes significant in HfNbTaTiZr at 300–1200 K.
Oxidation effects become significant in oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr at 300–1200 K.
HfNbTaTiZr has a disordered bcc phase structure relevant to oxygen-defect interactions.
The presence, distribution, and nature of oxygen-induced defects mediate transport behavior through interactions with the bcc alloy structure.
Oxygen-related defects introduce additional charge-carrier and phonon scattering channels that control effective conductivity.
At low temperatures, oxygen-defect scattering reduces conductivity relative to an ideal crystal.
At high temperatures, defect mobility and oxidation-related lattice distortions modulate conductivity.
The defect-inclusive model will predict lower conductivity than a defect-free model in the 0–200 K regime.
The defect-inclusive model will reproduce the complex 300–1200 K conductivity dependence of specimens containing 1 wt.% oxygen more closely than defect-free models.
The defect-inclusive model will reduce mean absolute conductivity-prediction error by at least approximately 20% relative to the defect-free model.
The proposed model is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen content near 1 wt.% at temperatures up to 1200 K.
At higher oxygen contents or temperatures above 1200 K, phase instability, oxidation, or microstructural changes may reduce model accuracy.
Failure to achieve at least a 20% error reduction on a held-out conductivity benchmark around 500 K would falsify the claimed accuracy advantage.
